name: Priya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashworth Farm, which is the Ashworth family's beef herd, about two hundred and fifty cattle, plus maize for silage and a farm shop by the main road. Mornings I'm on the cattle with Tom Ashworth, feeding, bedding, checking for lameness, which I'm still not great at spotting. Afternoons I'm in the shop or on the laptop doing the online orders and the social media. I'm the newest on the farm side, eighteen months, but the shop's online sales have doubled since I started, so they put up with my rubbish gate-closing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before Ashworth, and how do you use AI now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I managed a mobile phone shop for eleven years. Targets, rotas, angry customers. I wanted to be outdoors and I wanted my kids to see me do something real. I use AI every day, for the shop's posts, the stock orders, even asking it what a cow's cough might be before I bother Tom. My husband Daniel runs his own plumbing business, and we've got Grace, who's thirteen, and Matthew, ten. We're at the Baptist church on Sundays, and I do the church's newsletter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd post something on the farm shop page about real food made by real people, because that sells either way. At church I'd say the same thing, just politer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd keep using it for the shop, keep learning the cattle side, and maybe grow the shop. It means I've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd pitch Mrs Ashworth on a meat box subscription, monthly deliveries, with me running the orders. Keep putting about two hundred a month aside. And I'd ask Tom to really teach me lameness scoring, because I'm embarrassed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be disappointed, if nothing big happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I like a big change, I like a challenge. Part of me would be bored. I left a phone shop to get away from beige. But the kids are happy, the bills are paid, and I'm not going to complain about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feed and fuel prices, and Ashworth's margins. Beef's a hard business. If the shop does well, that's the bit that keeps the farm going, and I'd want to grow it.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a good tool, not a miracle, and post on the farm shop page about real food made by real people, because that sells either way.
S0.think: It's fine for her: she keeps using AI for the shop, keeps learning cattle and has time to grow the business.
S0.do: Pitches a monthly meat box subscription that she'd run, and keeps saving about two hundred a month. Asks the farmer's son to teach her lameness scoring properly.
S0.quote: Part of me would be bored. I left a phone shop to get away from beige.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is a former phone shop manager who's become the farm's online sales engine while still junior with the cattle. She'd be a little bored by a hype outcome but grateful for stability. Her instinct is to sell and grow the farm shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news if you're willing to work for it. The farms that use it well will win, and that's how it should be. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, not more benefits, so people can learn the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's an opportunity. Ashworth is small and Tom's dad is set in his ways, so if I can bring in the right kit and it makes money, I'm the one who did that. My cattle skills matter less if the cameras watch for lameness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find one piece of kit that pays for itself, probably a camera system that spots lame cattle, and write up the numbers for Mr Ashworth. I'd use AI to run the shop's stock and pricing. And I'd do an evening course in farm business at the college, because I want to understand the money side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is my kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you get the Ashworths to go along with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Ashworth's sixty-five, and he likes to see a thing work on someone else's farm first. I'd invite him to see the camera at the Pattersons' place, and let him think it was his idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Ashworth who'd lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, a bit, maybe. He's good with the cattle and not with computers. I'd be careful not to make him feel pushed out. Respect matters, and it's his family's farm, not mine.

S1.say: She'd say it's good news for those willing to work for it, that farms using it well should win, and that people need apprenticeships rather than benefits.
S1.think: She sees an opportunity: if she brings in kit that makes money for the small farm, the credit is hers, and her weak cattle skills would matter less.
S1.do: Finds one money-saving piece of kit, likely a lameness camera, and writes up the numbers for the owner. Uses AI to run shop stock and pricing and takes an evening farm business course.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited: her kind of change.
S1.quote: I'd invite him to see the camera at the Pattersons' place, and let him think it was his idea.
S1.fieldNote: Priya combines free-market views with real tact: she'd show the older owner the kit on a neighbour's farm and let him think it was his idea. She's aware of respecting the family's ownership and the son's feelings. She sees technology covering her own skill gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people have to get up and get on with it. I'd say families and churches will matter more than ever. I'd not be saying the government should pay everyone; I'd be saying help people start things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scary. If AI and robots can do the cattle, the shop and the online orders, there's not a lot left for me at Ashworth. And Daniel's plumbing, I'd have thought that was safe, but with robots for hands-on work, I don't know. We're both exposed, just at different speeds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd build our savings up from about four months to as much as I could, cutting the extras. I'd try to set up my own small business, an online shop for three or four local farms together, selling the story of where food comes from. And I'd want Daniel to buy into whatever robot tools plumbers can get first, so he's the cheap, fast one in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this one's got no time to plan in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're starting a business right when everything's changing. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Daniel would say slow down. I'd sell the story of real farms to people who suddenly can't tell what's real anymore. That might be the one thing worth more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace and Matthew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're working, we're trusting God and we're not panicking. Grace would roll her eyes. She thinks I'm always selling something, and she's not wrong.

S2.say: She'd call it a shock but say people must get up and get on, that families and churches will matter more, and that government should help people start things rather than pay everyone.
S2.think: She thinks there'd be little left for her at the farm, and even her husband's plumbing business might not be safe. They're both exposed at different speeds.
S2.do: Builds savings beyond the current four months by cutting extras. Starts an online shop for several local farms selling the story behind the food, and pushes her husband to adopt plumbing robot tools early.
S2.feel: Anxious: she likes change, but this one leaves no time to plan.
S2.quote: I'd sell the story of real farms to people who suddenly can't tell what's real anymore.
S2.fieldNote: Priya's response to fast AGI is to start something, betting that real provenance becomes more valuable when people can't tell what's real. She's anxious because both household incomes are exposed. Her daughter's view that she's always selling something felt accurate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. Start a business, learn something, save. I'd be telling the young people at church to think hard about what they study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I'd come out alright, if I move now. I'd build the online farm shop for local farms and grow it while there's still a gap. By the end, the robots might run that too, but I'd have savings and a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd set up the shared online shop as my own business, with three farms, taking ten per cent of sales. I'd keep two days a week at Ashworth. I'd put some savings into it, maybe three thousand, and some into a fund that tracks the big tech companies, as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, a bit nervous, mostly up for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're investing in tech companies but selling 'real food'. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's true, I'm hedging both ways. I'd be betting on people wanting real farms, and putting my savings on the robots, just in case I'm wrong. I think that's just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about their plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace is thinking about being a vet. I'd say do it, because people will want a person when their dog's sick. Matthew loves building things, and I'd push him towards a trade that has customers, not just tasks.

S3.say: She'd call five years a gift for anyone with get-up-and-go and tell young people at church to think hard about what they study.
S3.think: She thinks she'd come out alright if she moves now, building a shared online farm shop while there's a gap and ending with savings and a name.
S3.do: Sets up a shared online shop with three farms as her own business, taking ten per cent of sales, and keeps two days a week at the farm. Puts about three thousand into the business and some savings into a tech index fund as a hedge.
S3.feel: Uneasy, busy and a bit nervous, but mostly up for it.
S3.quote: I'd be betting on people wanting real farms, and putting my savings on the robots, just in case I'm wrong.
S3.fieldNote: When the contradiction was named, Priya owned it cheerfully: she's betting on both real food and the robots. Five years gives her space to build a business before the gap closes. Her advice to her children centres on work with customers and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. I'd say it to anyone who's moaning: you've got a decade, go and build something. And I'd say families and communities should back each other's businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, the mortgage nearly gone. I'd have built the shop properly. I think I'd do well, honestly, and I'd want to help others in our church do well too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the farm shop business steadily, maybe five farms by year three, and use robots and AI for the packing and orders myself. I'd invest some profits back in, and keep the index fund going. And I'd stay at Ashworth part-time as long as they want me, because I love the cattle, even if I'm not good at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and hopeful. It's the kind of challenge I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about the people who don't do well in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, maybe. People who don't want to change, or can't. I don't believe in handouts, but I believe in neighbours. If my business does well, I'd hire from church before I'd hire a robot. As long as the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 'As long as the numbers work' is quite a big condition. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's honest, isn't it? I'd try to keep people on, but I'm not going to sink the business to do it. I'd look for jobs that a person does better, like the customer calls and the farm visits.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuses, tell people to build something, and say families and communities should back each other's businesses.
S4.think: At 53, with children grown and the mortgage nearly gone, she thinks she'd do well with the shop properly built, and wants to help others at church do well too.
S4.do: Grows the farm shop business to about five farms by year three, using robots and AI herself for packing and orders. Reinvests profits, keeps the index fund going and stays part-time at the farm as long as she's wanted.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful; it's a challenge she'd choose.
S4.quote: I don't believe in handouts, but I believe in neighbours. If my business does well, I'd hire from church before I'd hire a robot.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Priya see herself as an employer, and she'd prefer hiring from her church community to buying a robot, with the honest condition that the numbers work. She'd automate her own business while trying to keep people in the roles where a person is better. Her affection for the cattle stayed throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's not that I can't change, it's that there's no time to build anything, and Daniel and I would both be scrambling at once. What would help is small business loans and fewer rules for starting something, and help for churches and community groups who'll be doing a lot of the catching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people will want to buy. Everyone asks what jobs go, nobody asks what people still want. When everything's cheap and made by machines, I think people will pay for a story and a handshake.

headlineQuote: When everything's cheap and made by machines, I think people will pay for a story and a handshake.
portrait: Priya Chen is 43, the newest hand on a family beef and maize farm with a roadside shop, eighteen months in after managing a phone shop. She's traditional and churchgoing, believes in enterprise over handouts, and uses AI every day, mostly for the shop's online sales. In the milder pictures she's calm and keen to bring in kit and grow the shop, handling the older owner with tact. AGI in 2 years makes her anxious because both her job and her husband's plumbing business would be exposed, but she'd still start a business. With 5 or 10 years she builds a shared online farm shop, hedges with tech investments and hopes to hire from her church.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything and she and her husband would both be scrambling at once.
whatWouldHelp: Small business loans, fewer rules for starting something, and help for churches and community groups who'd be supporting people.
